column1: What is the official number of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act adopted in 2024?
column2: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

column1: What are the two main legal bases in the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) underpinning the AI Act?
column2: Article 114 (internal market) and Article 16 (protection of personal data).

column1: What is the main objective of the AI Act?
column2: To improve the functioning of the internal market while promoting human-centric and trustworthy AI, with a high level of protection for health, safety and fundamental rights.

column1: How does Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 define an “AI system”?
column2: A machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy, capable of adapting its behaviour and inferring outputs (such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions) from inputs.

column1: What key feature distinguishes an AI system from traditional automated software?
column2: Its ability to infer—derive models, algorithms or outputs beyond simple rules coded exclusively by humans.

column1: Under the AI Act, what is a “provider” of an AI system?
column2: A natural or legal person, public authority or body that develops an AI system (or has it developed) and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark.

column1: Under the AI Act, what is a “deployer” of an AI system?
column2: A natural or legal person, public authority or body that uses an AI system under its authority, except for use in a personal, non-professional activity.

column1: Does the AI Act apply to providers established in a third country (outside the EU)?
column2: Yes, if they place AI systems on the EU market or put them into service in the EU, or if the output produced by the system is used in the EU.

column1: Are AI activities carried out exclusively for military or national defence purposes covered by the AI Act?
column2: No. AI systems used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes are entirely excluded from its scope.

column1: Are scientific research and development activities on AI systems, before they are placed on the market, subject to the AI Act?
column2: No. Systems developed and put into service exclusively for scientific research and development are excluded.

column1: Is an individual's personal and non-professional use of an AI system subject to the obligations imposed on deployers?
column2: No. Strictly personal and non-professional use is excluded.

column1: What type of regulatory approach does the AI Act take to govern artificial intelligence?
column2: A risk-based approach, with requirements calibrated according to the severity of potential risks.

column1: Why are AI practices using subliminal or manipulative techniques that significantly distort a person's behaviour prohibited?
column2: Because they impair free will and informed decision-making unconsciously, causing significant harm.

column1: Under Article 5, may an AI system exploit a group's vulnerability due to age or disability?
column2: No. Exploiting such vulnerabilities in a way that causes significant harm is strictly prohibited.

column1: What is the prohibited AI practice known as “social scoring”?
column2: Evaluating or classifying people based on their social behaviour in ways that lead to unfavourable treatment in unrelated contexts or treatment that is disproportionate.

column1: Is assessing a person's risk of committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or personality traits permitted?
column2: No. Predictive criminal-risk assessments based solely on the profiling of natural persons are prohibited.

column1: Why is creating or expanding facial-recognition databases through untargeted scraping of images prohibited?
column2: Because it creates a sense of mass surveillance and seriously violates fundamental rights, particularly the right to privacy.

column1: Are AI systems designed to infer people's emotions prohibited in every context?
column2: No. They are specifically prohibited in workplaces and educational institutions, except for medical or safety reasons.

column1: What type of biometric categorisation is strictly prohibited by Article 5 of the AI Act?
column2: Biometric categorisation used to infer sensitive attributes, such as race, political opinions, religious beliefs or sexual orientation.

column1: Is the real-time remote biometric identification of people in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes prohibited?
column2: Yes, in principle. There are only narrowly defined and strictly regulated exceptions, such as searching for victims, addressing imminent threats or pursuing serious offences.

column1: What prior authorisation is required to use real-time remote biometric identification in an exceptional law-enforcement case?
column2: Prior authorisation from a judicial authority or an independent administrative authority of a Member State.

column1: In a duly justified emergency, what is the maximum time limit for requesting the required judicial authorisation for real-time biometric identification?
column2: No later than 24 hours.

column1: What are the two categories of AI systems classified as “high-risk” under Article 6?
column2: 1) Safety components of products subject to third-party conformity assessment under EU harmonisation legislation (Annex I); 2) Stand-alone AI systems listed in Annex III.

column1: Under what derogation may an AI system listed in Annex III NOT be considered high-risk (Article 6(3))?
column2: If it poses no significant risk to health, safety or fundamental rights, in particular because it does not materially influence the outcome of a decision.

column1: Can an Annex III AI system that performs profiling of natural persons benefit from the derogation for non-significant risk?
column2: No. An AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always considered high-risk.

column1: Which biometric systems are classified as high-risk under point 1 of Annex III?
column2: Remote biometric identification systems, biometric categorisation systems that infer sensitive attributes, and emotion-recognition systems (where permitted).

column1: Why are AI systems used in the management of critical infrastructure (water, gas, electricity and road traffic) classified as high-risk?
column2: Because a failure or malfunction of their safety component could endanger people's lives and health on a large scale.

column1: Give two examples of high-risk AI uses in education and vocational training (Annex III, point 3).
column2: 1) Selecting or admitting pupils/students; 2) Assessing learning outcomes; 3) Monitoring prohibited behaviour during exams.

column1: Which types of AI systems used in employment are classified as high-risk (Annex III, point 4)?
column2: Systems used for recruitment (screening applications), decisions on promotion or dismissal, task allocation, or monitoring performance.

column1: Are AI systems used to assess the creditworthiness of natural persons high-risk? What is the exception?
column2: Yes, they are high-risk. The exception is AI systems used to detect financial fraud.

column1: Why are AI systems used to triage emergency calls or prioritise emergency services classified as high-risk?
column2: Because they make critical decisions that directly affect people's lives, health and the protection of property.

column1: When is an AI system used in the administration of justice classified as high-risk?
column2: When it assists a judicial authority in researching and interpreting facts and the law, and applying the law to a specific case.

column1: What does the “risk management system” requirement for high-risk AI involve?
column2: A continuous, iterative process planned throughout the system's lifecycle to identify, assess and mitigate known or foreseeable risks.

column1: What qualities must the training, validation and testing datasets for high-risk AI systems have?
column2: They must be relevant, sufficiently representative and, to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the system's intended purpose.

column1: To correct discriminatory bias, may providers of high-risk AI process special categories of personal data?
column2: Yes, exceptionally, where strictly necessary to detect and correct bias, subject to appropriate safeguards for individuals.

column1: What technical automatic-logging capability must a high-risk AI system include during operation?
column2: The ability to automatically record events in logs to ensure traceability.

column1: What is the purpose of the transparency and instructions-for-use requirements for high-risk AI?
column2: To enable deployers to understand how the system works, assess its capabilities and limitations, and make informed decisions.

column1: What does the principle of human oversight require for high-risk AI systems?
column2: The system must be designed so that competent natural persons can monitor its operation, intervene or stop it when necessary.

column1: What enhanced human verification requirement applies to remote biometric identification?
column2: No action or decision may be taken solely on the basis of the identification result without separate confirmation by at least two natural persons.

column1: Besides accuracy and robustness, what major technical requirement protects high-risk AI systems against malicious attacks?
column2: Cybersecurity, including resistance to data-poisoning and reverse-engineering attacks.

column1: What is an “authorised representative” under the AI Act?
column2: A natural or legal person established in the EU who has received a written mandate from a provider located outside the EU to carry out its regulatory obligations.

column1: Under Article 27, who must conduct a “fundamental rights impact assessment” (FRIA) before first using a high-risk AI system?
column2: Deployers that are public-law bodies, private entities providing public services, or those using certain specific systems (credit and insurance).

column1: What is the difference between a “general-purpose AI model” (GPAI model) and an “AI system”?
column2: A GPAI model is a foundational component capable of a wide range of tasks; it needs interfaces or other components to become a functional AI system.

column1: What cumulative training-compute threshold creates a presumption that a general-purpose AI model poses “systemic risk”?
column2: A cumulative amount of computation exceeding 10²⁵ floating-point operations (FLOPs).

column1: Name two legal obligations imposed on providers of general-purpose AI (GPAI) models.
column2: 1) Draw up and maintain technical documentation; 2) Make information available to downstream providers; 3) Comply with EU copyright law; 4) Publish a summary of training content.

column1: Are GPAI models released under free and open-source licences exempt from certain requirements? What is the exception?
column2: Yes. They are exempt from extensive technical-documentation requirements, UNLESS they pose systemic risk.

column1: What obligation applies to providers of AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons (Article 50(1))?
column2: To inform people that they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious from the context.

column1: How must AI-generated audio, image, video or text content be marked by the provider?
column2: In a machine-readable format and in a way that can be detected as artificially generated or manipulated (digital marking/watermarking).

column1: How does the AI Act define a “deepfake”?
column2: AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing people, objects or events and would falsely appear authentic to a person.

column1: What is a deployer's obligation when using an AI system that generates a “deepfake”?
column2: To disclose publicly that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

column1: What is an “AI regulatory sandbox”?
column2: A controlled framework established by a competent authority that allows innovative AI systems to be developed, trained and tested under regulatory supervision.

column1: Is every EU Member State required to establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox?
column2: Yes. Each Member State must ensure that at least one operational sandbox is available (jointly with other Member States if necessary) by 2 August 2026.

column1: What conditions must be met to test a high-risk AI system in real-world conditions outside a sandbox?
column2: Draw up a real-world testing plan, obtain the informed consent of participants, and ensure that decisions can be fully reversed.

column1: What is the role of the European AI Office within the Commission?
column2: To develop EU expertise, coordinate the implementation of the regulation and supervise general-purpose AI models.

column1: Who makes up the European Artificial Intelligence Board?
column2: One representative from each Member State, with the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) participating as an observer, alongside the AI Office.

column1: What is the purpose of the EU database for high-risk AI systems (Article 71)?
column2: To publicly list registered high-risk AI systems, submitted by providers and public deployers before they are put into use.

column1: Under Article 86, what right does a person have when subject to an individual decision based on high-risk AI?
column2: The right to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the AI system's role in the decision-making process.

column1: When do the prohibitions on unacceptable-risk AI practices become applicable?
column2: 2 February 2025 (six months after the Act entered into force).

column1: When do the obligations governing general-purpose AI (GPAI) models and governance become applicable?
column2: 2 August 2025 (12 months after the Act entered into force).

column1: What is the general date of application of the AI Act as a whole?
column2: 2 August 2026 (24 months after the Act entered into force).
